screens.title: What is HDA Versioning?
screens.narratorSegment: Versioning an HDA means creating distinct definitions of the same named asset so different scenes can rely on the version they were built with. A version number like 1.0, 1.1, or 2.0 is more than a label — it is a contract. When you increment a version and save a new. hda definition, Houdini retains the old definition so scenes saved with v1.0 keep working. This provides safety: teams can introduce new features or bug fixes without forcing immediate upgrades. Concretely, imagine a modular building generator used across levels. You want to add a new door type but not change the shape algorithm in existing levels. Bump the version to 1.1, save the new definition, and new scenes will use 1.1 while old level files remain on 1.0. A common misconception is that incrementing a version is optional for any change. In practice, small cosmetic parameter tweaks might not need a new major version, but structural or behavior changes should. Keep your versioning policy documented: what constitutes a patch, a minor feature, or a breaking change. That policy lets artists decide whether to upgrade and preserves reproducibility of renders and game builds. Key takeaway: use version numbers as explicit communication to your team about compatibility and risk.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › HDA Versioning
Versioning — clear definition
A version is a saved HDA definition on disk. Houdini keeps old definitions so scenes continue to reference the version they were created with. This enables safe, non-destructive updates.
Why it matters
  • Prevents unexpected behavior when assets change.
  • Provides rollback points if a new version introduces bugs.
  • Communicates compatibility expectations to your team.
Common mistake
Not incrementing a version for breaking changes, which silently replaces older behavior and can break saved scenes.
Concrete example
You maintain a modular building HDA at v1.0 used across multiple levels. You add a new algorithm for window placement that changes geometry. Save a new definition as v2.0 so older levels continue referencing v1.0 while new designers can opt into v2.0.
Key takeaway
Version numbers are contracts. Use them strategically to control risk and communicate compatibility.
Check your understanding
If you change display-only labels on parameters, do you always need to increment the major version? Think about whether the change affects behavior or only usability.

screens.title: Versioning Workflow — Increment & Save
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the concrete steps you will use to create a new HDA version. Start by selecting the HDA instance in your scene and opening Type Properties. In the Basic tab find the Version field, update it from 1.0 to 1.1 or 2.0 depending on the scope of the change, then Apply and Accept. Next, if you made edits inside the asset you must persist them: right-click the HDA node and choose Save Node Type. This writes the updated. hda file to disk under the new version. Houdini stores the old definition as well, so existing scenes referencing v1.0 continue to work. A common trap is making internal changes while leaving the version number unchanged — that can silently overwrite previous behavior if you save to the same definition. Another important action is Match Current Definition: after saving, use Match Current Definition to ensure the instance's lock state and definition match the saved. hda. Practically, treat version updates like releases: document changes in the asset’s Help tab, update the version number, save the node type, and commit the. hda file to your version control. That sequence gives you reproducibility and a clear audit trail for the change.

Decide change scope

02
Update Version in Type Properties

Example Scenario
You add a new noise generator inside your HDA that changes mesh shape. This is a behavior change: increment the version to 2.0, save the node type, and commit the new .hda so artists know how to opt into the new algorithm.
Pitfall

screens.title: Locking vs Allow Editing — Understanding the Difference
screens.narratorSegment: Locking an HDA is a protective measure: a locked asset prevents changes to its internal node network so users can't accidentally alter behavior. In production this is the recommended default because it preserves predictability. When you need to change internals, use Allow Editing of Contents. That action temporarily unlocks that instance and lets you dive into the internal nodes and make edits. But it's important to understand the distinction between making local instance edits and updating the shared HDA definition. If you unlock an instance and make changes without saving the node type, your edits remain local to that instance and will not update the. hda file on disk. That leads to divergence and possible loss of work if the scene is opened on another machine. After editing, the correct sequence is Save Node Type to write the definition, then Match Current Definition to re-lock and align instances. A common misconception is to think unlocking automatically writes changes back to the shared library — it does not. Unlocking is a permission to change; saving is the deliberate act that creates a new, shared definition. Keep this distinction in your workflow to avoid hidden overrides and inconsistent team results.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Locking & Editing
Locked by default
Locked HDAs protect internal networks so users can't accidentally change behavior in production scenes.
Allow Editing
Temporarily unlock an instance to modify internals. Changes are local until you Save Node Type.
Misconception
Unlocking does not automatically update the shared definition. You must explicitly save to persist edits.
Example: local override
You allow editing and change a noise height from 0.2 to 1.0 on an instance. Unless you Save Node Type, that change stays local and other users with the shared .hda won't see it.
Best practice
Only unlock when necessary. After edits, save the node type and use Match Current Definition to re-lock the instance cleanly.
Pro tip

Document why you unlocked and what you changed in the asset Help tab before saving and checking in.

screens.title: Editing and Saving — A Safe Sequence
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson prescribes a reliable sequence when you need to modify an HDA. First, discuss the change with your team if it's shared or critical. Then right-click the HDA instance and select Allow Editing of Contents to open the internal network. Make targeted changes — fix a node parameter or replace a SOP — then test the instance in representative scenes. Next, save your work by right-clicking the HDA node and selecting Save Node Type. This writes the updated definition to the. hda file on disk and captures the change in a shareable form. Immediately after saving, use Match Current Definition on the instance to realign the node's stored definition and re-lock it. Finally, commit the new. hda file to version control with a descriptive message that explains the change and the version bump. A common mistake is skipping the Match Current Definition step; this can leave instances in a mismatched state where the UI shows edits but the stored definition differs. By following this sequence you ensure edits are deliberate, testable, and propagated in a controlled way that other team members can consume without surprises.

Skipping version control commit after saving, which leaves the new .hda untracked and creates confusion about which version is authoritative.

screens.title: Distributing HDAs and HOUDINI_PATH
screens.narratorSegment: Distribution means making. hda files available to other users so an HDA appears in their Tab menu and scene instances resolve. The simplest method is manual: copy the. hda file to the target machine or project folder. For teams, set up a centralized shared HDA library on a network drive and add that directory to the HOUDINI_PATH environment variable. Houdini scans HOUDINI_PATH at startup and exposes any. hda definitions it finds. You can add paths directly in a houdini. env file for project-specific configuration, or via your custom launcher script. Use relative paths when possible for project-contained assets so moving a project doesn't break references. If an HDA instance becomes unresolved, the usual fix is to verify HOUDINI_PATH includes the directory where the. hda resides or to manually point the instance's Definition File parameter to the correct file. A common pitfall is copying. hda files into inconsistent locations across team members; this leads to unresolved instances and version mismatches. Best practice: store the shared HDA library in version control or a consistent network path, document where to add it to HOUDINI_PATH, and include a short houdini. env example in project onboarding. This makes asset distribution repeatable and dependable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Distribution & HOUDINI_PATH
Shared HDA library architecture
Keep .hda files in a central folder scanned by Houdini. Add that folder to HOUDINI_PATH so everyone sees the assets without copying them into each project.
houdini.env example
HOUDINI_PATH = C:/Project/SharedHDAs;<$HOUDINI_PATH>
Place houdini.env in the Houdini preferences or project folder to configure paths for the team.
Unresolved HDA fix
If an instance is unresolved, check that the .hda exists at a path listed in HOUDINI_PATH or update the instance's Definition File to the correct .hda. Consistent paths avoid this problem.
Manual copy
Copy the .hda into another machine's project folder to share quickly, but use this sparingly for teams to avoid divergence.
Best practice
Store shared HDAs in version control and document HOUDINI_PATH setup in project onboarding materials.
Key Takeaway

A single, versioned shared HDA library and consistent HOUDINI_PATH settings keep assets resolved and teams synchronized.

screens.title: Referencing External .hda Definitions
screens.narratorSegment: When you place an HDA into a scene, Houdini creates an instance that points to a definition file on disk. That connection is the asset's definition reference. If the definition file is moved, renamed, or deleted, the instance becomes unresolved. Unresolved means Houdini cannot find the. hda file the instance expects, and the node will show errors or a red indicator. A reliable way to avoid this is to standardize where HDAs live and how they are referenced. Use project-relative paths where possible and keep a shared HDA library for cross-team projects. A concrete example: an HDA created in a project's hda folder using a relative path like./hdas/cohortia_simple_box. hda will remain resolvable if the whole project folder is moved intact. Contrast that with an absolute path pointing to a user-specific folder; moving the project will break the link. A common misconception is thinking Houdini bundles the definition inside the scene; it does not. The scene stores a reference to the definition. If you see an unresolved HDA, check that the definition file exists, verify HOUDINI_PATH entries, or manually update the Definition File parameter in Type Properties. Takeaway: keep paths stable, prefer relative project paths, and confirm everyone’s HOUDINI_PATH when sharing assets.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Referencing External .hda
Definition Reference
What the scene stores for each HDA instance
Houdini stores a pointer to the HDA's definition file on disk. If that file is missing or moved, the instance becomes unresolved. Maintain consistent storage locations and use project-relative paths whenever feasible to keep instances stable across machines.
Quick Troubleshooting
Steps to resolve an unresolved HDA
  • Confirm the .hda file still exists at the expected path.
  • Check HOUDINI_PATH includes the containing directory.
  • Open Type Properties → Basic → Definition File to point to a new location if needed.
Example: Definition File Path
A path the instance uses to find its .hda
Definition File: ./hdas/cohortia_simple_box.hda
Using a relative path like this ties the HDA to the project layout rather than a single user's folder. If the whole project is copied or moved, the reference remains valid.
Common Mistake
Relying on absolute, user-specific paths when saving HDAs. These break when the project moves or when another user loads the scene.
Key Takeaway
Keep definition paths consistent and share HDAs via a shared library so instances remain resolvable.

screens.title: Managing Paths and the Definition File Parameter
screens.narratorSegment: Paths determine whether an HDA stays linked as projects move between machines. Prefer project-relative folders for HDAs so the entire project can be moved without breaking references. A practical pattern is to have an hda directory at the root of the project and reference definitions with relative paths. For shared team libraries, add the shared directory to HOUDINI_PATH so Houdini discovers the files automatically. If an instance becomes unresolved, you can manually repair it: open the node's Type Properties and look in the Basic tab for the Definition File parameter. Point this to the correct. hda on disk or choose the relative path used by your project. A concrete example is copying cohortia_simple_box. hda to a central hda folder and then updating team members’ houdini. env to include that folder. Misconceptions happen when users assume Houdini embeds the definition into the scene; instead, the scene references the external file. Another subtle point: when you update a definition file in place and Houdini finds multiple versions, instances will stay on their saved version until explicitly matched or upgraded. So updating a shared definition requires clear communication and version increments to avoid silently changing other users' scenes. Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Path Management
Path Strategies
Clear rules for where HDAs live
  • Project-relative hda folder (recommended for single-project assets).
  • Central shared HDA library added to HOUDINI_PATH for cross-project teams.
  • Avoid user-specific absolute paths when saving definitions.
  • Document the chosen layout in project setup notes or houdini.env.
These rules reduce unresolved HDAs and speed onboarding for new team members.
Repair Guide
  1. Open the HDA node and choose Type Properties → Basic.
  2. Check the Definition File parameter to see the recorded path.
  3. Point it to the correct .hda or copy the .hda into the expected project folder.
  4. Restart Houdini if you changed HOUDINI_PATH to ensure a fresh scan.
Example houdini.env entry
HOUDINI_PATH = C:/Projects/MyGame/hdas;&HOUDINI_PATH
Adding the shared folder here makes HDAs appear in the Tab menu for all users who use that houdini.env.

screens.title: Version Control Workflow for HDAs
screens.narratorSegment: Collaborative HDA development succeeds when you treat. hda files like any other source artifact. Use your existing version control system to track changes and communicate intent. A practical workflow looks like this: check out or lock the. hda in version control, unlock the HDA in Houdini by allowing editing of contents if necessary, make your internal fixes or feature additions, increment the version number in Type Properties for any significant change, save the node type to write the updated. hda, and then commit the new file with a clear message describing the update. This preserves backward compatibility: scenes referencing v1.0 will continue to use it while the repository holds v1.1 or v2.0 as a separate definition. An important contrast: do not make local overrides in production scenes and assume they will propagate. Local edits to an unlocked instance without saving the node type are local overrides and will not update the shared. hda. A common misconception is that saving the node type automatically updates other users' scenes; it does not. They will continue to reference their saved version until they choose to match the new definition. For critical assets, assign an owner and use code-review or an approval step before committing major changes. This practice prevents accidental breaking changes and builds shared confidence in the asset lifecycle.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Version Control Workflow
Recommended Step Flow
A repeatable team-safe sequence
  1. Lock or check out the .hda in your VCS to signal intent.
  2. Allow editing of contents on the HDA instance to change internals.
  3. Make changes, test the asset in representative scenes, and verify backward compatibility.
  4. Increment the Version value for significant changes in Type Properties.
  5. Right-click → Save Node Type to write the updated .hda to disk.
  6. Commit the new .hda with a descriptive message and inform the team.
This avoids silently overwriting previous definitions and gives other artists a clear upgrade path.
Avoid this mistake
Editing instance internals without saving the node type and assuming changes propagated. Those edits remain local overrides unless you save and commit the .hda.
Pro tip
Use a single HDA owner and a small review process for critical assets to prevent regressions and coordinate version bumps.

screens.title: Documenting HDAs and the Help Tab
screens.narratorSegment: Good documentation turns an HDA into a usable tool rather than a mystery. Houdini provides a Help tab in Type Properties where you can add descriptions, usage hints, and parameter explanations. Include a short purpose statement, recommended inputs, common parameter ranges, and a link to external design notes if your team uses a central wiki. A concrete example: for a procedural building HDA, list recommended scale ranges, which parameters control openings, and which toggles are expensive to compute. That helps artists avoid unintended performance costs. Another best practice is to document expected folder structure and how to add the HDA to HOUDINI_PATH so other team members can load it quickly. Misconceptions include thinking comments inside internal nodes are sufficient; internal node comments disappear if the asset is locked and do not surface to users browsing the Tab menu. Use the Help tab for user-facing guidance and keep a separate developer log in your version control commits for internal change notes. Finally, consider small usage examples or screenshots localized into the Help tab so users can see a before/after quickly. Good documentation reduces support overhead and increases asset adoption.

screens.title: Simulate Distribution and Troubleshoot HOUDINI_PATH
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a distribution simulation and some troubleshooting steps you can do quickly. First, locate your cohortia_simple_box. hda in your project hda folder. Copy it into a new shared folder, for example C:/Temp/MySharedHDAs. Next, simulate a teammate who cannot see the asset: on their machine open a terminal and check the environment variable that tells Houdini where to look. Run a command to echo the HOUDINI_PATH and inspect whether the shared folder is included. If it is missing, add an entry to houdini. env or update the system HOUDINI_PATH to include the share, then restart Houdini so it rescans for definitions. If an HDA still appears unresolved, open the HDA instance in the scene and use Type Properties → Basic → Definition File to see the stored path. If the path points to a now-missing location, either move the. hda back or update the Definition File to the current location. Common mistakes include forgetting to restart Houdini after changing houdini. env and assuming Tab menu visibility updates instantly. Also avoid keeping local overrides in scenes; after you fix the definition, consider using Match Current Definition on instances to clean local differences. This sequence helps you distribute assets while understanding and repairing the most frequent path and resolution issues.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Distribution & Troubleshooting
Step-by-step Simulation
  1. Copy cohortia_simple_box.hda to C:/Temp/MySharedHDAs.
  2. On the other machine, run a terminal check for HOUDINI_PATH to see if the folder is listed.
  3. If missing, add the folder to houdini.env or the system HOUDINI_PATH and restart Houdini.
  4. If unresolved, open the instance and update Definition File to point to the new .hda location.

echo $HOUDINI_PATH
# or on Windows (PowerShell): $env:HOUDINI_PATH
If the output doesn't include your shared folder, Houdini won't find the copied .hda until you add it and restart.

A simple copy + HOUDINI_PATH update is enough to distribute an HDA. Restart Houdini and repair Definition File entries when needed to resolve broken instances.

Versioning an HDA means creating distinct definitions of the same named asset so different scenes can rely on the version they were built with. An unresolved HDA occurs when Houdini cannot find the definition file an instance references; the fix is to restore the file, update HOUDINI_PATH, or repoint the Definition File. Finally, collaborative best practices include using version control, documenting assets in the Help tab, and assigning an HDA owner responsible for maintenance. This combination of discoverability, versioned changes, and clear ownership prevents accidental breakage and speeds onboarding for artists who use the assets. Keep these principles in mind when you prepare HDAs for broader team consumption.
